segments.text: American Fork City Council — Regular Session — August 25, 2026:

Aaron Booker, a nonresident, criticized what he viewed as inconsistent enforcement of meeting decorum and a broader pattern of selective enforcement within the City and Police Department. He urged City officials to apply standards equally, protect First Amendment rights, and pursue meaningful reform.
View minutes, page 1

Daniel Sroka urged the City to take action to restore public trust in the Police Department, suggesting policy revisions, improved body cameras, or a resident review board. Citing public critiques of body-camera footage, Mr. Sroka called for meaningful reform and emphasized the importance of protecting constitutional rights.
View minutes, page 2

Debbie Shaw described her family’s longstanding service to American Fork and raised concerns about alleged civil-rights violations involving her son and others. She requested a fair, transparent, and independent review of the Police Department and urged City leadership to restore public trust through accountability and action.
View minutes, page 2

Jan Chamberlain, a member of the NO ICE in Utah County Coalition, requested a meeting with City officials to discuss immigration enforcement policies. She supported lawful due process while encouraging a humanitarian approach that protects innocent immigrants and children. She also asked the City to consider policies limiting the use of municipal property and local law-enforcement resources for federal immigration enforcement.
View minutes, page 2

Mary Mitchell, an American Fork resident, supported an independent review of the Police Department and urged the city to rebuild public trust, particularly among vulnerable and immigrant communities. She requested greater transparency regarding the Police Department’s cooperation with ICE under Utah County’s 287(g) Agreement, citing concerns about racial profiling and residents becoming afraid to contact law enforcement.
View minutes, page 2

Roy Shaw, an American Fork resident, requested an independent third-party review of the Police Department’s accountability, leadership, and handling of alleged misconduct. He stated that the review should determine whether systemic or leadership failures exist, restore public confidence, and guide any appropriate personnel action. He also expressed concern that similar requests from residents had received no meaningful response.
View minutes, page 2
Andrea Tamita, a 93-year-old American Fork citizen, urged City officials and residents to address wrongdoing, hold public officials and safety patrols accountable, and protect children.
View minutes, page 3

Elizabeth Oscarson, an American Fork resident, opposed ICE activity within the city and stated that residents deserve to feel safe. She requested complete transparency and public reporting regarding interactions between City departments and federal immigration authorities.
View minutes, page 3

Gregory Titus stated that his and his wife’s constitutional rights had been violated in American Fork. He expressed a willingness to work with City officials and invited them to contact him regarding his concerns.
View minutes, page 3

entities.speaker: Anna Montoya
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Ms. Montoya summarized that the interim budget included a proposed $660,000 property-tax increase to partially staff a new fire station. She reported that insurance-premium savings would allow the Council to reduce the proposed increase while maintaining the planned staffing. She noted that the Council could reduce the increase further, but any additional reduction would require corresponding changes to other budget items.
View minutes, page 4

entities.speaker: Clark P. Taylor
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Council Member Taylor stated that he remained reluctant to support a property-tax increase but recognized that rising costs made it difficult for the City to continue providing essential services, particularly public safety, without additional revenue. He opposed using reserves for ongoing expenses and said he intended to support a reduced 5.7% increase.
View minutes, page 4

entities.speaker: Ernie John
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Council Member John opposed using reserves to fund ongoing operations and supported the reduced tax-increase proposal. He later emphasized that supporting the increase was not an easy decision and said residents he had spoken with generally preferred smaller, more manageable increases instead of waiting several years and facing a substantial adjustment.
View minutes, pages 4 and 6

entities.speaker: Ryan Hunter
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Council Member Hunter said the proposal was consistent with comments residents made during the 2021 Truth in Taxation process favoring smaller, incremental adjustments instead of infrequent, substantial increases. He cautioned against treating annual increases as automatic and emphasized that each adjustment should still receive careful scrutiny and consideration of the burden placed on taxpayers.
View minutes, pages 5–6

entities.speaker: Staci Carroll
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Council Member Carroll acknowledged that increasing taxes was difficult even when the need was clear. She explained that staffing the new fire station was a high priority because firefighter salaries were an ongoing operating expense that had to be permanently included in the budget. She said providing 24-hour public-safety coverage justified the additional cost and that she would support the reduced 5.7% increase.
View minutes, page 5

entities.speaker: Tim Holley
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Council Member Holley stated that he would vote against a property-tax increase because residents were already facing substantial increases in household expenses. He said he had proposed several alternatives and remained dissatisfied with how the purpose and proposed use of the increase had been communicated. Although he respected the other Council members' positions, he said he could not support the increase in good conscience.
View minutes, page 6

entities.speaker: Bradley J. Frost
entities.remark-context: Final 2026 property-tax rate and FY 2027 budget

segments.text: Mayor Frost stated that the budget process, which began in February, would conclude that evening. He emphasized that the budget was one of the Council's most important responsibilities because it established priorities and funded services affecting residents.
View minutes, page 7
